methodology: The study used the ABAQUS (2022) software with a three-dimensional nonlinear finite element method to analyze beam models using GFRP reinforcements with diameters of 10 mm and 12 mm, concrete strengths of 25 MPa and 40 MPa, and different stirrup spacings.
research_objective: To reveal the interactive effects of reinforcement diameter, concrete strength, and stirrup spacing through numerical analyses and contribute to existing research.

key_findings.finding: Increasing GFRP bar diameter from 10 mm to 12 mm significantly enhanced load-carrying capacity and ductility.
Higher concrete strength (C40) improved initial stiffness and delayed cracking.
Reducing stirrup spacing from 100 mm to 50 mm increased structural stability and delayed damage.
GFRP reinforcement contributes to increased flexural stiffness and improved crack resistance in reinforced concrete beams.
Numerical model predictions aligned well with experimental data for GFRP-reinforced beams under various conditions.
Increasing the reinforcement ratio leads to improvements in bending capacity, while also causing significant reductions in crack width and displacement.
GFRP bars can serve as a viable supplement to conventional steel reinforcement for improving flexural stiffness and reducing deflection at mid-span.
The combined use of GFRP reinforcement and ECC material provides an effective structural system in terms of both strength and ductility.
Torsion cracks started later for beams reinforced with GFRP compared to control samples.
